vsm1.4:67.1: Here is the explanation of the meaning.
vsm1.4:67.2: When a too clever bee learns that a flower on a tree is blooming,
vsm1.4:67.5: and arrives when the pollen is finished;
vsm1.4:67.6: and another, not clever enough bee, who sets out with too slow a speed, arrives when the pollen is finished too;
vsm1.4:67.7: but a clever bee sets out with balanced speed,
vsm1.4:67.8: arrives with ease at the cluster of flowers,
vsm1.4:67.9: takes as much pollen as it pleases
vsm1.4:68.1: Again, when a surgeon’s pupils are being trained in the use of the scalpel on a lotus leaf in a dish of water,
vsm1.4:68.2: one who is too clever applies the scalpel hurriedly
vsm1.4:68.3: and either cuts the lotus leaf in two
vsm1.4:68.4: or pushes it under the water,
vsm1.4:68.5: and another who is not clever enough
vsm1.4:68.6: does not even dare to touch it with the scalpel for fear of cutting it in two or pushing it under;
vsm1.4:68.7: but one who is clever shows the scalpel stroke on it by means of a balanced effort,
vsm1.4:68.8: and being good at his craft
vsm1.4:68.9: he is rewarded on such occasions.
vsm1.4:69.1: Again when the king announces, “Anyone who can draw out a spider’s thread four fathoms long shall receive four thousand,”
vsm1.4:69.2: one man who is too clever breaks the spider’s thread here and there by pulling it hurriedly,
vsm1.4:69.3: and another who is not clever enough does not dare to touch it with his hand for fear of breaking it,
vsm1.4:69.4: but a clever man pulls it out starting from the end with a balanced effort, winds it on a stick, and so wins the prize.
vsm1.4:70.1: Again, a too clever skipper hoists full sails in a high wind and sends his ship adrift,
vsm1.4:70.2: and another, not clever enough skipper, lowers his sails in a light wind and remains where he is,
vsm1.4:70.3: but a clever skipper hoists full sails in a light wind,
vsm1.4:70.4: takes in half his sails in a high wind,
vsm1.4:70.5: and so arrives safely at his desired destination.
vsm1.4:71.1: Again, when a teacher says, “Anyone who fills the oil-tube without spilling any oil will win a prize,”
vsm1.4:71.2: one who is too clever fills it hurriedly out of greed for the prize, and he spills the oil,
vsm1.4:71.3: and another who is not clever enough does not dare to pour the oil at all for fear of spilling it,
vsm1.4:71.4: but one who is clever fills it with a balanced effort and wins the prize.
vsm1.4:72.1: Just as in these five similes, so too when the sign arises,
vsm1.4:72.2: one bhikkhu forces his energy, thinking “I shall soon reach absorption.”
vsm1.4:72.3: Then his mind lapses into agitation because of his mind’s over-exerted energy and he is prevented from reaching absorption.
vsm1.4:72.4: Another who sees the defect in over-exertion slacks off his energy, thinking, “What is absorption to me now?”
vsm1.4:72.5: Then his mind lapses into idleness because of his mind’s too lax energy and he too is prevented from reaching absorption.
vsm1.4:72.6: Yet another who frees his mind from idleness even when it is only slightly idle
vsm1.4:72.7: and from agitation when only slightly agitated,
vsm1.4:72.8: confronting the sign with balanced effort,
vsm1.4:72.10: One should be like the last-named.
vsm1.4:73.1: It was with reference to this meaning that it was said above:
vsm1.4:73.2:
“Well-controlled bees get the pollen;
Well-balanced efforts meet to treat
Leaves, thread, and ships, and oil-tubes too,
Gain thus, not otherwise, the prize.
vsm1.4:73.3:
Let him set aside then this lax
Also this agitated state,
Steering here his mind at the sign
As the bee and the rest suggest”.
vsm1.4:74.1: So, while he is guiding his mind in this way, confronting the sign,
vsm1.4:74.3:
there arises in him mind-door adverting with that same earth kasiṇa as its object, interrupting
the occurrence of consciousness as life-continuum, and evoked by the constant repeating of “earth, earth.”
vsm1.4:74.4:
After that, either four or five impulsions impel on that same object, the last
one of which is an impulsion of the fine-material sphere.
vsm1.4:74.5:
The rest are of the sense sphere, but they have stronger applied thought, sustained thought,
happiness, bliss, and unification of mind than the normal ones.
vsm1.4:74.6:
They are called “preliminary work” consciousnesses because they are the preliminary work for absorption; and they
are also called “access” consciousnesses because of their nearness to absorption because they happen in its neighbourhood,
just as the words “village access” and “city access” are used for a place near to a village,
etc.; and they are also called “conformity” consciousnesses because they conform to those that precede
the “preliminary work” consciousnesses and to the absorption that follows.
vsm1.4:74.7: And the last of these is also called “change-of-lineage” because it transcends the limited sense-sphere lineage
vsm1.4:74.8: and brings into being the exalted fine-material-sphere lineage.
vsm1.4:75.1: But omitting repetitions, then either the first is the “preliminary work,”
vsm1.4:75.8: Then either the fourth in the latter case or the fifth in the former case is the absorption consciousness.
vsm1.4:75.9: For it is only either the fourth or the fifth that fixes in absorption.
vsm1.4:75.10: And that is according as there is swift or sluggish direct-knowledge.
vsm1.4:76.1:
But the Abhidhamma scholar, the Elder Godatta, quoted this text: “Preceding profitable states are a condition,
as repetition condition, for succeeding profitable states” (Paṭṭh I 5).
vsm1.4:76.2:
Adding, “It is owing to the repetition condition that each succeeding state is strong,
so there is absorption also in the sixth and seventh.”
vsm1.4:77.1: That is rejected by the commentaries with the remark that it is merely that elder’s opinion,
vsm1.4:77.2: adding that, “It is only either in the fourth or the fifth that there is absorption.
vsm1.4:77.3: Beyond that, impulsion lapses. It is said to do so because of nearness of the life-continuum.”
vsm1.4:77.4: And that has been stated in this way after consideration, so it cannot be rejected.
vsm1.4:77.5:
For just as a man who is running towards a precipice and wants to stop cannot do
so when he has his foot on the edge but falls over it,
vsm1.4:77.6: so there can be no fixing in absorption in the sixth or the seventh because of the nearness to the life-continuum.
vsm1.4:77.7: That is why it should be understood that there is absorption only in the fourth or the fifth.
vsm1.4:78.1: But that absorption is only of a single conscious moment.
vsm1.4:78.2: For there are seven instances in which the normal extent of the cognitive series does not apply.
vsm1.4:78.3: They are in the cases of the first absorption,
vsm1.4:78.7: life-continuum jhāna in the fine-material and immaterial kinds of becoming,
vsm1.4:78.8: the base consisting of neither perception nor non-perception as condition for cessation of perception and feeling,
vsm1.4:78.9: and the fruition attainment in one emerging from cessation.
vsm1.4:78.10: Here the fruition next after the path does not exceed three consciousnesses in number;
vsm1.4:78.11: the consciousnesses of the base consisting of neither perception nor non-perception as condition for cessation
vsm1.4:78.12: do not exceed two in number;
vsm1.4:78.13: there is no measure of the number of consciousnesses in the life-continuum in the fine-material and immaterial kinds of becoming.
vsm1.4:78.14: In the remaining instances the number of consciousnesses is one only.
vsm1.4:78.15: So absorption is of a single consciousness moment.
vsm1.4:78.16: After that, it lapses into the life-continuum.
vsm1.4:78.17: Then the life-continuum is interrupted by adverting for the purpose of reviewing the jhāna,
vsm1.4:78.18: next to which comes the reviewing of the jhāna.
vsm1.4:79.1: The First Jhāna At this point, “Quite secluded from sense desires, secluded from unprofitable things
vsm1.4:79.2:
he enters upon and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained
thought with happiness and bliss born of seclusion” (Vibh 245),
vsm1.4:79.3: and so he has attained the first jhāna, which abandons five factors, possesses five factors,
vsm1.4:79.4: is good in three ways, possesses ten characteristics, and is of the earth kasiṇa.
vsm1.4:80.1: Herein, quite secluded from sense desires means having secluded himself from,
vsm1.4:80.3: having gone away from, sense desires.
vsm1.4:80.4: Now, this word quite (eva) should be understood to have the meaning of absoluteness.
vsm1.4:80.5:
Precisely because it has the meaning of absoluteness it shows how, on the actual
occasion of entering upon and dwelling in the first jhāna,
vsm1.4:80.6: sense desires as well as being non-existent then are the first jhāna’s contrary opposite,
vsm1.4:80.7: and it also shows that the arrival takes place only (eva) through the letting go of sense desires.
vsm1.4:81.1: When absoluteness is introduced thus, “quite secluded from sense desires,” what is expressed is this:
vsm1.4:81.2: sense desires are certainly incompatible with this jhāna; when they exist, it does not occur,
vsm1.4:81.3: just as when there is darkness, there is no lamplight;
vsm1.4:81.4: and it is only by letting go of them that it is reached, just as the further bank is reached only by letting go of the near bank.
vsm1.4:81.5: That is why absoluteness is introduced.
vsm1.4:82.1: Here it might be asked: But why is this word “quite” mentioned only in the first phrase and not in the second?
vsm1.4:82.2: How is this, might he enter upon and dwell in the first jhāna even when not secluded from unprofitable things?
vsm1.4:82.3: It should not be regarded in that way.
vsm1.4:82.4: It is mentioned in the first phrase as the escape from them;
vsm1.4:82.5:
for this jhāna is the escape from sense desires since it surmounts the sense-desire
element and since it is incompatible with greed for sense desires,
vsm1.4:82.6: according as it is said: “The escape from sense desires is this, that is to say, renunciation” (D III 275).
vsm1.4:82.7:
But in the second phrase the word eva should be adduced and taken as said, as in the passage,
“Bhikkhus, only (eva) here is there an ascetic, here a second ascetic” (M I 63).
vsm1.4:82.8:
For it is impossible to enter upon and dwell in jhāna unsecluded also from unprofitable
things, in other words, the hindrances other than that sense desire.
vsm1.4:82.9: So this word must be read in both phrases thus: “Quite secluded from sense desires, quite secluded from unprofitable things.”
vsm1.4:82.10: And although the word “secluded” as a general term
vsm1.4:82.11: includes all kinds of seclusion, that is to say, seclusion by substitution of opposites, etc., and bodily seclusion, etc.,
vsm1.4:82.12: still only the three, namely, bodily seclusion, mental seclusion, and seclusion by suppression (suspension) should be regarded here.
vsm1.4:83.1:
But this term “sense desires” should be regarded as including all kinds, that is to say, sense desires as object as given
in the Niddesa in the passage beginning, “What are sense desires as object? They are agreeable visible objects …” (Nidd I 1),
vsm1.4:83.2:
and the sense desires as defilement given there too and in the Vibhaṅga thus: “Zeal as sense
desire (kāma), greed as sense desire, zeal and greed as sense desire, thinking as sense desire,
greed as sense desire, thinking and greed as sense desire” (Nidd I 2; Vibh 256).
vsm1.4:83.3: That being so, the words “quite secluded from sense desires” properly mean “quite secluded from sense desires as object,”
vsm1.4:83.5:
while the words “secluded from unprofitable things” properly mean “secluded from sense
desires as defilement or from all unprofitable things,”
vsm1.4:83.7:
And in this case giving up of pleasure in sense desires is indicated by the first since
it only expresses seclusion from sense desires as object,
vsm1.4:83.8:
while acquisition of pleasure in renunciation is indicated by the second since it
expresses seclusion from sense desire as defilement.
vsm1.4:84.1:
And with sense desires as object and sense desires as defilement expressed in this way, it should also be recognized
that the abandoning of the objective basis for defilement is indicated by the first of these two phrases
vsm1.4:84.2: and the abandoning of the subjective defilement by the second;
vsm1.4:84.3: also that the giving up of the cause of cupidity is indicated by the first
vsm1.4:84.4: and the giving up of the cause of stupidity by the second;
vsm1.4:84.5: also that the purification of one’s occupation is indicated by the first and the educating of one’s inclination by the second.
vsm1.4:84.6: This, firstly, is the method here when the words from sense desires are treated as referring to sense desires as object.
vsm1.4:85.1:
But if they are treated as referring to sense desires as defilement, then it is simply just zeal for sense
desires (kāmacchanda) in the various forms of zeal (chanda), greed (rāga), etc.,
vsm1.4:85.2: that is intended as “sense desires” (kāma) (§83, 2nd quotation).
vsm1.4:85.3: And although that lust is also included by the word “unprofitable,”
vsm1.4:85.4:
it is nevertheless stated separately in the Vibhaṅga in the way beginning, “Herein, what are sense desires?
Zeal as sense desire …” (Vibh 256) because of its incompatibility with jhāna.
vsm1.4:85.5: Or, alternatively, it is mentioned in the first phrase because it is sense desire as defilement
vsm1.4:85.6: and in the second phrase because it is included in the “unprofitable.”
vsm1.4:85.7: And because this lust has various forms, therefore “from sense desires” is said instead of “from sense desire.”
vsm1.4:86.1: And although there may be unprofitableness in other states as well,
vsm1.4:86.2:
nevertheless only the hindrances are mentioned subsequently in the Vibhaṅga thus, “Herein, what states are unprofitable?
Lust …” (Vibh 256), etc., in order to show their opposition to, and incompatibility with, the jhāna factors.
vsm1.4:86.3: For the hindrances are the contrary opposites of the jhāna factors:
vsm1.4:86.4: what is meant is that the jhāna factors are incompatible with them, eliminate them, abolish them.
vsm1.4:86.5: And it is said accordingly in the Peṭaka (Peṭakopadesa): “Concentration is incompatible with lust,
vsm1.4:86.7: applied thought with stiffness and torpor,
vsm1.4:86.9: and sustained thought with uncertainty” (not in Peṭakopadesa).
